ENT Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: 4-day history of intensely itchy, red, sore rash; no clear trigger identified (no new soaps, detergents, clothing reported).
- Symptom timeline and progression: Sudden onset 4 days ago; persistent, worsening pruritus interfering with sleep and work; OTC topical steroid and OTC antihistamine provided no relief.
- ENT symptoms: Denies throat swelling/closure sensation, voice change/hoarseness, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling, ear pain/hearing changes, neck pain/swelling.
- Distribution of rash: Chest, hands, inner elbows; no facial or leg involvement.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: Prior eczema limited to arms; prior topical steroid & emollient regimen effective in past; no prior hospital visits for similar complaint.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergies: “None known.”
  • Current meds: None regular. OTC topical steroid cream (name/dose not documented), OTC antihistamine (type/dose not documented) used without benefit.
- Social context: Lives with several flat-mates; 31-year-old male; full-time project manager in a pharmaceutical company; non-smoker; occasional alcohol (few beers/week).

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: Video consult—provider reports erythematous, dry, cracked rash on chest, hands, inner elbows; no facial swelling.
- Airway/breathing: Patient denies breathing difficulty; no stridor or noisy breathing noted.
- Mental status/associated features: Sleep disturbance due to pruritus; otherwise alert.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient: Not stated.

Assessment:
Working impression: Likely atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare.
Evidence summary: Prior history of eczema; distribution includes flexural areas; intense pruritus; dry, cracked skin; no systemic features.
DDx (consistent with transcript):
1. Atopic dermatitis flare – high likelihood given past history and characteristic features.
2. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – moderate likelihood; acute onset, new distribution; no confirmed exposure (opposing evidence).
3. Scabies infestation – lower likelihood; severe pruritus and hand involvement but rapid onset and lack of burrows/contacts reducing probability.

Plan:
- Prescriptions:
  • Potent topical corticosteroid (stronger than OTC preparation) – apply thinly to affected areas BID for 7–10 days.
  • Emollient bath/shower additive and moisturizer – liberal application multiple times daily.
  • Oral antihistamine, Fexofenadine (prescription strength) – 180 mg PO daily (dose per clinician’s statement) to reduce itch.
- Self-care / trigger management:
  • Keep skin well-hydrated; avoid hot showers/soaps with fragrance or dye.
  • Maintain diary of potential triggers (detergents, clothing, environmental exposures).
- Escalation / red-flags:
  • Seek urgent care for spreading rash with pain, pus, fever, or if new airway symptoms develop (throat tightness, voice change, breathing difficulty).
- Follow-up:
  • Review in 1 week if no improvement or sooner if worsening.
  • Consider dermatology referral if refractory or if alternate diagnoses (e.g., scabies, contact dermatitis) emerge.
  • Patient advised to inform flat-mates and seek assessment for them as well if any start itching (scabies possibility, though presently low).

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing elements: No vital signs; no full skin or ENT exam details (lesion morphology, lymph nodes); exact names/doses of previously tried OTC creams/antihistamines not documented; no documentation of family history of atopy; no photos for teledermatology comparison.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Audio intermittently unclear but key clinical details captured; no major omissions detected.
